title: Divorce, Remarriage and the Church
excerpt: Jesus spoke about divorce more severely than most churches now do, the church has read him in three different ways for most of its history, and it has managed to fail both the marriages it should have guarded and the people it should have protected.
body:
Four people can sit in the same row on a Sunday and hear the word divorce four ways. One was left, years ago, and still takes a seat near the back because of how the room went quiet the first time she came alone. One has married again and is happy, and now and then reads a verse in Matthew and wonders what God calls his marriage. One went to a pastor to say that her husband hits her, and was told to pray harder and go home. And one couple ended a marriage because they had grown apart, and nobody in their church said a word about it, then or since.

The skeptic watching them has a pointed observation. The church speaks loudly about some matters of sex and marriage and has gone almost silent about this one, though Jesus said a great deal more about this one. That observation is fair.

One thing has to be said before any of the argument. If you are in danger, get safe first and sort the theology after. If you're in immediate danger, call 911. If you need someone sooner, [Find Help](/help) lists hotlines for abuse and sexual assault.

## The Law of Moses and the Two Schools

The law of Moses has one main passage on divorce, and it does not command divorce or even set out the grounds for it. It takes for granted that divorce happens. A man finds "some indecency" in his wife, "writes her a certificate of divorce and puts it in her hand and sends her out of his house" (Deuteronomy 24:1), and she marries someone else. The law's ruling is narrow: if the second marriage ends, the first husband may not take her back (Deuteronomy 24:4). The certificate mattered. In a world where a woman alone had almost no means of support, it was her proof that she was free to marry again.

Everything turned on the two Hebrew words translated "some indecency," and by the time of Jesus the teachers of Israel had divided over them. The Mishnah, the collection of rabbinic rulings written down around the year 200, preserves the argument. The school of Shammai held that a man may not divorce his wife unless he has found unchaste behavior in her. The school of Hillel held that he may, in the words of one English translation, "even if she spoiled his food." A generation after Jesus, Rabbi Akiva added that it was enough if the man found another woman more attractive. Only the husband could write the certificate.

The prophets had already spoken to the men who used that freedom. Malachi, around the fifth century before Christ, tells husbands that God no longer accepts their offerings "because the LORD was witness between you and the wife of your youth, to whom you have been faithless, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant" (Malachi 2:14). The next verse but one is among the most quoted in this whole debate, and its Hebrew is difficult. The King James Version has God say "that he hateth putting away." Many modern Bibles give the famous form, in which God says he hates divorce. The English Standard Version reads the hatred as the husband's: "the man who does not love his wife but divorces her, says the LORD, the God of Israel, covers his garment with violence" (Malachi 2:16). On every one of these readings the target is the same. It is a man who discards the wife who trusted him. Malachi calls that violence. The verse was never a stick for beating the woman who was discarded.

## What Jesus Said

When the Pharisees came to Jesus, they asked Hillel's question: "Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?" (Matthew 19:3). He would not answer inside the terms of the debate. He went back behind Moses to creation: "So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matthew 19:6). When they pointed to the certificate in Deuteronomy, he told them what kind of law it was: "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so" (Matthew 19:8). Moses had regulated a wrong. He had not blessed it.

Then comes the sentence the church has argued over ever since. "And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery" (Matthew 19:9). The exception appears in Matthew, here and in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:32). In Mark and Luke there is none: "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her" (Mark 10:11).

Two things in those sentences were new. A husband in that world did not commit adultery against his wife; adultery was an offense against another man. Jesus says "against her," and with two words gives the wife a claim on her husband's faithfulness equal to his on hers. And the disciples, who had grown up with Hillel's rule, were appalled: "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry" (Matthew 19:10). They understood him to be saying something hard. The woman who could be sent away for a spoiled dinner was the person his hardness protected.

Paul adds one case Jesus had not addressed. Writing to Corinth, he repeats the Lord's charge that husband and wife should not divorce, and then, speaking on his own authority as an apostle, turns to marriages where only one partner has come to faith. The believer is not to leave. "But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace" (1 Corinthians 7:15).

Those are the texts. Christians who honor all of them have built three different houses on them.

## Three Readings, Each in Its Own Words

The first Christians were strict. A Roman Christian writing known as the Shepherd of Hermas, from the second century, considers a husband whose wife persists in adultery. He must separate from her. But he must not marry again: "The husband should put her away, and remain by himself. But if he put his wife away and marry another, he also commits adultery." The reason given is striking. He stays unmarried so that she can repent and come back. Hermas adds that "In this matter man and woman are to be treated exactly in the same way."

The Catholic Church built on that foundation, and Augustine gave it its reasoning. Writing around 401, he argued that marriage carries a bond that survives even a legal divorce, so "that the compact of marriage is not done away by divorce intervening." In its own terms the Catholic position is this. A valid marriage between two baptized people, once consummated, is a sign of Christ's union with the church, and Christ does not divorce the church. No power on earth can dissolve it. Spouses may live apart for serious cause, and the Council of Trent in November 1563 defended the church's teaching that "a separation may take place between husband and wife." But the same council condemned the claim that the church errs in teaching "that the bond of matrimony cannot be dissolved on account of the adultery of one of the married parties." An annulment is a different thing from a divorce. It is a finding that, because of some defect in consent or capacity at the start, a true marriage never came to be. Catholics know how hard this teaching is. They hold it because they believe it is what Jesus said.

The Orthodox churches of the East begin in the same place. Marriage is meant to be one and unbroken. But they have long reasoned that a marriage can die, killed by adultery or by something as grave, and that the church, acting as a physician, may in mercy permit a second marriage. The Greek word for this is *oikonomia*, economy: the household management of a pastor who bends the strict rule for the healing of a person without pretending the rule has changed. A second marriage has traditionally been celebrated with prayers of repentance and with less festivity than the first. Basil of Caesarea, setting down rules for his clergy in the 370s, already assigns a period of penance to those who marry a second time. The Orthodox would say that they hold the ideal as firmly as Rome and treat the failure more as a wound than a legal status.

The Protestant Reformers took a third path. The scholar Erasmus had argued in the 1510s that the exception in Matthew allowed the innocent spouse to marry again, and the Reformers agreed. If Jesus named an exception, they reasoned, it is an exception to the whole sentence, the remarrying as well as the divorcing. To Matthew's ground they joined Paul's. The Westminster Confession of 1647 states the result: "nothing but adultery, or such wilful desertion as can no way be remedied by the Church or civil magistrate, is cause sufficient of dissolving the bond of marriage." Where the divorce is for adultery, it says, the innocent party may "marry another, as if the offending party were dead."

Protestants have not stayed in one room since. Some evangelical scholars have returned to something like the early church's position, arguing that Jesus allowed separation and not remarriage. Others have argued from the marriage duties named in Exodus 21:10–11 and from Paul's "not enslaved" that abuse and hard-hearted neglect break the covenant as surely as adultery and desertion do. Most Protestant churches still stand near Westminster.

Each house has a fear about the others. The Catholic fears that every exception becomes a door, and that the doors multiply until the vow means nothing. The Protestant fears that a rule without the exceptions Jesus and Paul gave binds the innocent to the sins of the guilty. The Orthodox fear that both have turned a mystery into a legal code.

## Abuse, and What No Tradition Requires

On one point the old writers must be heard so that they can be refused. In the same letter in which Basil lays down his rules, he considers a wife who has left her husband. "In the case of her being beaten, and refusing to submit," he writes, "it would be better for her to endure than to be separated from her husband." He notes, to his credit, that custom in his day was harder on wives than on husbands and that the Lord's words apply "to men and women alike." But the sentence about beating stood, and versions of it were said to women for sixteen hundred years. Some are saying it still.

It is not what Scripture says. None of these passages tells you to stay in danger. Paul's own rule for the wife assumes she may have to leave: "the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband)" (1 Corinthians 7:10–11). Trent defended separation "for many causes." Not one of the three traditions teaches that a person must remain under the same roof with someone who is harming them or their children. They differ on whether the marriage bond can be ended and whether another marriage may follow. They do not differ on whether you may get out of the house.

And the Bible's picture of the husband leaves no room for the man who uses his place in the home as a weapon. "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25). A man who beats his wife has not exercised authority. He has broken his vow, and in Malachi's phrase he has covered his garment with violence. Whether that breach frees her to marry again is a question on which faithful pastors disagree. Whether it is her sin to leave is not.

## What We Have Done

We have failed in two directions, and usually in the same congregations.

We made peace with easy divorce. Beginning around 1970 the laws of one state after another were rewritten so that either spouse could end a marriage without proving any wrong, and the church, which had the words of Jesus, mostly adjusted. We stopped preaching on it because too many of our people were touched by it. We learned to say that a couple had grown apart, as if a covenant were a climate. The disciples heard Jesus and said it would be better not to marry. We have arranged things so that nobody in our pews is ever that startled.

And we sent the abused home. We told women that their suffering was their cross, that a quieter spirit would change him, that divorce was the one thing God hates. We disciplined the wife who left and kept the husband in leadership. We did the opposite of what Malachi did. He spoke for the wife against the man who wronged her.

Then, having been lax where Jesus was strict and strict where he was tender, we treated the divorced as a caste. The same churches that said nothing while a marriage died found their voice once it was over, and used it on the person sitting alone.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

All Christians confess that God made marriage, that he meant it to join one man and one woman for life, and that to break a marriage is to tear something he joined. Jesus put that beyond dispute. No tradition treats divorce as a neutral event.

The grounds on which a marriage may be ended, and whether either party may marry again, are questions of the second order. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians answer them differently while reciting the same creed, and Protestants answer them differently among themselves. This essay has set the answers side by side and does not choose among them.

What to do about a particular marriage is not something a page can decide. That belongs to a person who knows the facts, in a church that holds a considered position, and it belongs first to the safety of anyone who is in danger.

If you are grieving a marriage that ended, you are not a second-class Christian. Grace is not the reward for a clean history. Jesus once sat by a well with a woman who had had five husbands and was living with a man who was not her husband (John 4:18). He told her the truth about her life, and he did not leave. She was the first person in her town to tell anyone about him.

Scripture goes further than that. When the prophets wanted to say what Israel's unfaithfulness had done to God, they did not only reach for the picture of a judge. They reached for a husband who had been left. He says through Jeremiah that he sent faithless Israel away "with a decree of divorce" (Jeremiah 3:8), and through Isaiah he calls his people back "like a wife deserted and grieved in spirit" (Isaiah 54:6). The God who says that what he has joined no one should separate knows this grief from the inside. He did not stop at the decree. He came after the one who left, and it cost him the cross.

*"So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."* (Matthew 19:6)

*"The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit."* (Psalm 34:18)
